hints: Picture one triglyceride in your head: one glycerol backbone with three fatty acid tails attached. Do those three tails have to be identical?
Remember how glycerol joins to a fatty acid (condensation to form an ester bond) and whether that type of bond is covalent, plus whether hydrophobic means polar or non-polar.
walkthrough:
**Recall the basic structure**

Think of a triglyceride as one small glycerol molecule holding three fatty acid chains.
Each of the three positions can hold a different fatty acid, so saturated and unsaturated can mix.

**Recall the bonding and properties**

Glycerol joins to each fatty acid by condensation, releasing water and forming an ester bond.
An ester bond is a type of covalent bond. The long hydrocarbon tails make the whole triglyceride non-polar and hydrophobic.

**Choose the correct statement**

That means glycerol is joined to each fatty acid by a covalent (ester) bond, which matches option D.

options.A: False. The three fatty acids on one glycerol can be a mixture of saturated and unsaturated, they do not have to be all the same type.
options.B: False. Ester bonds are found inside one triglyceride, between glycerol and each fatty acid, not joining two whole triglycerides together.
options.C: False. This is a contradiction. Triglycerides are hydrophobic because they are non-polar, not polar.
options.D: Correct. Each fatty acid is linked to glycerol by an ester bond, and an ester bond is a covalent bond formed by condensation.
